<reason>Both sides built genuinely competitive cases with unusually clean framing. CON's "containment, not conscription" reframe was original and produced the debate's best single hit: convexity only reduces total harm if the peak actually falls, so if PRO concedes the core stays at capacity, diffusion duplicates a cost curve on streets that never opted in. CON also answered the elasticity trap credibly by distinguishing rationing a scarce bottleneck from relocating complements chosen for proximity. But PRO won the two decisive exchanges. First, PRO's Q1 on seasons exposed a real burden: a February visitor uses the same sights at near-zero crowding cost, so does CON actually oppose temporal spreading? CON's answer ("a February booking is not the proposition") was definitional and evasive, and CON's own closing plan explicitly invites visitors to "come off-peak to the same sights" — endorsing half the motion as written while denying it counts. Second, PRO successfully turned CON's answer to "where does the next visitor go?" CON accepted "another city, or stay home," and PRO crystallized that as containment having a turnstile rather than a capacity plan, while one district is permanently designated to absorb the scrum by design. CON's "the streets behind the basilica are the product, not a victim" bit the bullet rather than defusing it. PRO's "the icon is ninety minutes, the trip is forty hours" and "deliberate placement versus whatever a platform algorithm finds" gave concrete mechanisms rather than assertion. CON also incurred an execution cost with a clipped over-length rebuttal. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Pressure Q1 on seasons, and its follow-up flip: even granting CON's worst case that off-peak trips are purely additional, the "failure mode is the city earns more and nobody is trampled." CON's reply that a February booking "is not the proposition" while its own closing invites visitors to come off-peak left half the motion effectively conceded.</best_rebuttal>
